era_visual_canon.clothing: Mining-era miners and mill workers wear sweat-stained cotton work shirts, khaki or navy shorts and trousers, singlets, sturdy leather work boots and wide-brimmed felt or cloth hats, often dusted all over with fine fibre dust. There is no modern protective equipment. Migrant and Australian women wear light cotton print dresses, sandals or flat shoes and headscarves against heat and dust. Children wear simple cotton shorts, shirts and dresses, often barefoot. Government doctors, inspectors and company managers wear lightweight suits or shirt-and-tie with trousers, sometimes with a hat. In later decades lawyers, officials and Aboriginal Traditional Owners appear in contemporary civilian dress appropriate to their decade.
era_visual_canon.technology: Mining era (1937-1966): electromechanical crushing and fibre-processing mill machinery, belt drives, conveyors, hand tools, carbide and early electric lamps, valve radios, rotary-dial or wind-up telephones, manual typewriters, carbon-copy paper reports, film cameras producing black-and-white or sepia prints. NO digital displays, NO computers, NO plastic electronics, NO modern dust extraction or air-monitoring devices. Later decades bring analog then early digital office equipment. Only the 2000s-2020s period allows modern phones and computers, and only away from the mining-era scenes.
era_visual_canon.vehicles_machinery: Small propeller-driven passenger aircraft landing on a dirt airstrip. Period utility trucks, flatbed lorries and tip trucks dumping loads of tailings. Ore-hauling trucks and mill-yard machinery: crushers, conveyors, hoppers. Mining-era scenes have no paved highways and no modern four-wheel-drive SUVs. Later periods show demolition machinery (1986-1992), then permanent road barricades blocking abandoned access roads.
era_visual_canon.interiors: Cramped cottages of corrugated iron, timber and asbestos-cement sheeting, with simple furniture, iron beds and fans. A dusty mill-shed interior with machinery and airborne fibre. A small township hospital ward with iron beds and basic obstetric instruments. A one-room-style school, a church hall, mining and health department offices with timber desks, filing cabinets and typewriters. In later periods: courtroom wood panelling (1988), parliamentary committee rooms, and a modern interview setting surrounded by sepia family photographs.
era_visual_canon.forbidden_anachronisms: In mining-era scenes: no modern respirators, hazmat suits, high-visibility vests or hard hats with modern logos. No paved asphalt roads with painted markings in the 1937-1966 township. No modern SUVs, jet airliners, drones, solar panels, mobile phones, LED or flat-panel screens, plastic signage, or contemporary branded clothing. No green lawns or modern landscaping. Do not show the town with buildings or residents after its demolition and abolition.
era_visual_canon.materials_textures: Houses of corrugated sheet metal, timber and asbestos-cement sheeting. Loose, fibrous mining tailings spread as the surface of roads, yards, the airstrip, the schoolyard and public spaces. Raw fibrous mineral that frays and crumbles when handled, releasing fine powdery dust. Bare earth and rocky gorge ground. Tailings deposits washed into creek beds, pools and floodplains.
era_visual_canon.color_palette: Exterior: intense red earth and red dust everywhere, blue-grey fibrous tailings (inferred from the mineral's 'blue asbestos' name), a pale dust haze around the mill and grey weathered metal roofs. Interior colours are not documented.
era_visual_canon.scale_dimensions: A small, isolated desert township served by a short dirt airstrip for small propeller planes. Three mines produced about 150,000 tonnes of commercial asbestos, leaving more than three million tonnes of tailings. Today the official Wittenoom Asbestos Management Area covers 46,840 hectares, with contamination reaching down creek channels toward the Fortescue River catchment.
era_visual_canon.distinctive_features: An isolated red-earth Pilbara desert township whose own roads, yards, schoolyard and airstrip were literally paved with blue asbestos mining waste. It is now emptied, erased from maps and sealed off by permanent barricades as a vast toxic forbidden zone.
era_visual_canon.demographics: Mining era: Australian miners and mill workers, European displaced persons assigned by the federal government (1948-1951), European workers recruited privately by CSR from 1950, and Spanish migrant families arriving under the 1958 Spain-Australia migration agreement. These include miners, their wives and young children born or raised in the town. All workers wear dust-covered work clothes; women and children wear light cotton clothing. Later decades: a dwindling handful of remaining residents, Banjima Aboriginal Traditional Owners of the land, asbestos-disease victims and their advocates, lawyers and government officials.
era_visual_canon.visual_reference_availability: No dedicated visual research blocks were provided. All place descriptions come from WRITTEN sources, not from images verified here. These include migrant oral testimony (red earth, dust everywhere, tin/timber/asbestos-cement houses, small propeller plane, children handling fibre), official reports (1957 Board of Reference describing dust-covered workers and a dust cloud at the mill, environmental studies of tailings in creeks and floodplains, permanent barricades) and a former worker's testimony (tailings dumped on yards, school, kindergarten and churches). PHOTOGRAPHIC sources are mentioned only as private family archives: a family portrait showing a bandaged foot, a baptism photograph dated 1963-07-07, and sepia family photographs shown in an interview. These are not available here. Tailings colour is INFERENCE from the mineral name 'blue asbestos'. Scale figures come from official text (tonnages, 46,840 ha). Gorge topography is INFERENCE from place names. Group ethnicity comes from written records, not photographs.

condition_evolution.at_event: A living, operating mining town: a working mill wrapped in a thick dust cloud, and corrugated-iron, timber and asbestos-cement cottages on red earth. Company trucks dump tailings onto yards, roads, the schoolyard and the airstrip. Small propeller planes land on the dusty strip, and children play with fraying fibre amid fine dust settling on everything.
condition_evolution.later: From 1978 the town is deliberately shrunk. Between 1986 and 1992 buildings are demolished and the school, nursing post and police station close. The airport closes in 1993, power is cut in 2006 and the town is abolished and erased from maps in 2007. The last residents leave around 2022-2023 and remaining structures are demolished. What remains is a deserted, tailings-strewn landscape with asbestos washing down creek channels, sealed by permanent barricades across every access road.

periods.clothing: Prospectors and early miners in rough cotton work shirts, khaki trousers or shorts, braces, felt hats and heavy boots. Officials in wool or linen suits with hats.
periods.technology: Hand tools, small-scale crushing equipment, valve radios, manual typewriters and black-and-white film photography. No electronics.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Early motor trucks and utility vehicles on dirt tracks through red ranges, plus basic mine-head equipment in the gorges.
periods.interiors: Makeshift camp huts, corrugated-iron sheds, and government mining offices with timber desks and paper files.

periods.clothing: Mill workers and miners in dust-covered cotton shirts, shorts, singlets and boots with no respirators. Migrant women in cotton print dresses and headscarves. Children in simple cotton clothes, often barefoot. Health officials in lightweight suits and ties.
periods.technology: An operating asbestos mill with crushers and conveyors, rotary or wind-up telephones, valve radios, typewriters, carbon-copy reports and film cameras producing family prints.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Small propeller passenger aircraft on a tailings-surfaced dirt airstrip, company tip trucks dumping tailings onto yards and roads, flatbed lorries and period utes.
periods.interiors: Tin, timber and asbestos-cement cottages, a dusty mill shed, a small hospital ward, a schoolroom, a church, and a migrant ship's cabins and decks.

periods.clothing: Remaining residents in casual 1970s-80s shorts, T-shirts and work wear. Lawyers and judges in suits and court attire. Officials in office suits.
periods.technology: Analog telephones, electric typewriters, early photocopiers, paper legal files and film or early video news cameras.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Ageing utility vehicles, demolition excavators and trucks removing buildings, and light aircraft at the soon-to-close airstrip.
periods.interiors: Half-emptied houses, closing school, nursing post and police station, wood-panelled courtrooms and parliamentary hearing rooms.

periods.clothing: Contemporary civilian dress for lawyers, officials, Traditional Owners and visiting UN representatives. Environmental assessors in modern field clothing.
periods.technology: Modern office computers and phones in present-day interviews only. Warning signage and permanent road barricades at the site.
periods.vehicles_machinery: Modern field vehicles kept outside the barricades, plus permanent barriers across access roads to the former town and gorge.
periods.interiors: Present-day legal and government offices and a domestic interview room with sepia family photographs. No habitable interiors remain on site.

people_groups.who: Spanish migrant miners, their wives and their children who came to Wittenoom under the 1958 Spain-Australia migration agreement, including children born in the town who later became media professionals.
people_groups.where_when: Seen on the migrant ship from Málaga via Suez and in Wittenoom (1962-1966), in Madrid and Australia afterward (1966-1971), and decades later at a 1985 airport checkpoint, at a 1991 diagnosis and in present-day interviews.
people_groups.appearance: Southern European Spanish people with light olive to tanned skin, dark brown or black hair and Mediterranean features; the men have lean, hardened labourer builds.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Men wear dust-covered cotton work shirts, trousers or shorts and boots in the mine, and pressed shirts for photos. Women wear light cotton print dresses, headscarves, sandals and neatly set short hair. Children wear simple cotton shorts and dresses, often barefoot, with Sunday best for a baptism.
Working-class Madrid and Australian civilian dress of the 1970s-80s: open-collar shirts, slacks, knit cardigans, modest dresses and casual jackets for the grown children.
Contemporary casual or smart-casual clothing; elderly women in cardigans and blouses at home among sepia family photographs, and adult children in modern professional attire.

people_groups.who: Australian miners, mill workers, mill fitters and union (AWU) members employed in the Wittenoom mines and mill.
people_groups.where_when: Seen in the Wittenoom mines, gorges and mill from 1937 to 1966, notably in 1946-1959 award and dust-allowance disputes and in the 1957 Board of Reference inspection, and later as disease victims and claimants (1979-1989).
people_groups.appearance: Australian men mostly of Anglo-Celtic descent, with sun-reddened or deeply tanned skin, varied brown to fair hair and wiry or muscular manual-labour builds.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Sweat-stained cotton work shirts or singlets, khaki or navy shorts and trousers, heavy leather boots and felt or cloth hats, all coated in fine fibre dust, with no respirators.
Older, ill men in plain civilian shirts, trousers and cardigans, some in hospital gowns.

people_groups.who: European displaced persons assigned by the Australian federal government to work contracts in Wittenoom, and European workers recruited privately by CSR.
people_groups.where_when: Seen in the Wittenoom mines and mill under 1948-1951 government contracts and through CSR recruitment from 1950 onward.
people_groups.appearance: European men with pale to light skin tanning in the desert sun, varied hair colours and lean labourer builds.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Simple second-hand or issued cotton work shirts, trousers or shorts, boots and cloth caps or hats, all dust-covered from the mill.

people_groups.who: Australian prospectors who opened and owned the early crocidolite workings before ABA took over their interests.
people_groups.where_when: Seen in the Yampire and Wittenoom Gorges and the Hamersley Ranges from 1937 to 1943.
people_groups.appearance: Australian men of Anglo-Celtic descent with weathered, sun-tanned skin and rugged outdoor builds.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Rough cotton shirts with rolled sleeves, khaki trousers, braces, wide-brimmed felt hats and heavy boots.

people_groups.who: Managers of ABA and executives and chairmen of the parent company CSR, a firm from the sugar industry.
people_groups.where_when: Seen in company management roles and dust hearings from 1943 to 1966, including the 1949 manager hearing and the 1966 closure announcement, and in later litigation (1988-1989).
people_groups.appearance: Australian businessmen of Anglo-Celtic descent with fair to lightly tanned skin and neatly groomed hair.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Tailored business suits, white shirts, ties and felt hats, with short neatly parted hair.
Dark business suits and ties of the late 1980s.

people_groups.who: Australian state mines inspectors and engineers, public health doctors, health inspectors, a Public Health Commissioner, an industrial hygienist and labour arbitration and Board of Reference members.
people_groups.where_when: Seen at Wittenoom and in government offices from 1944 to 1968, including the 1944 dust report, 1948-1951 warnings, the 1957 mill inspection, the 1962 mesothelioma report, the 1965 schoolyard reprimand and the 1966 hygiene review.
people_groups.appearance: Australian professional men mostly of Anglo-Celtic descent with fair to sun-tanned skin and tidy short hair.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Lightweight suits or white shirts with ties and trousers, sometimes with a hat, carrying notebooks and paper reports; jackets come off during on-site inspections.

people_groups.who: Australian federal and Western Australian political figures and state government bodies, including a Prime Minister, a Lands Minister, parliamentary inquiry leaders and committee chairs.
people_groups.where_when: Seen in government settings in 1947, in the 1978 relocation policy, in the 1992 and 1994 parliamentary reports, in the 2006-2007 abolition, in 2016 and 2019 decisions and in 2023-2026 responses to the lawsuit.
people_groups.appearance: Australian politicians and officials, mostly of Anglo-Celtic descent, with fair skin and neatly groomed hair.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Dark wool or linen three-piece or two-piece suits, ties and felt hats.
1970s-90s business suits with wide or medium ties and conservative haircuts.
Contemporary business suits, open-collar shirts and smart office attire.

people_groups.who: Banjima Aboriginal Traditional Owners of the land, including an elder and activist and leaders of the Banjima Native Title Aboriginal Corporation.
people_groups.where_when: Seen on Banjima country around the Wittenoom area and in legal and advocacy settings from 2023 to 2026.
people_groups.appearance: Aboriginal Australian people with dark brown skin, dark wavy or curly hair, often greying in elders, and broad facial features.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Contemporary casual outback clothing such as collared shirts, T-shirts, jeans and broad-brimmed hats, with smart-casual shirts for legal and media appearances.

people_groups.who: Former workers, residents and family members affected by asbestos disease who founded the Asbestos Diseases Society of Australia, its leadership, and the lawyers who litigated against CSR and the State.
people_groups.where_when: Seen in Australian advocacy and court settings from 1979 through the 1988 verdict and the 1989 settlement, and in continuing advocacy and the 2026 Federal Court action.

clothing_by_period.clothing: Plain civilian shirts, slacks and dresses for victims, and dark suits and ties or court attire for lawyers.
Contemporary professional business attire for advocates and lawyers.

people_groups.who: The dwindling remaining residents of Wittenoom and members of the local Wittenoom Steering Committee after the mine closed.
people_groups.where_when: Seen in the shrinking town from 1978 through the 1986-1992 demolitions, with remaining residents in 2006 and the last departures in 2022-2023.
